title: Optimize walkthrough — KV hypothesis sandbox demo with Cerulean Ventures
topics: session affinity and warm KV hits
summary: Redwood AE + SE ran an Optimize-focused sandbox demo to validate a KV-prefetch hypothesis for Cerulean's sessionized chat product. Main goals: quantify token-cost savings from prefix/KV caching across three workload scenarios, demonstrate console simulator and sandbox, discuss deployment options (hosted vs dedicated vs private), and align next steps for pilot and security review.
action_items: Jordan Hayes|Send sandbox link and cost-sim spreadsheet|2026-09-20
Priya Raman|Run two additional sims with Cerulean’s 8k sequence distribution and share results|2026-09-23
Miguel Torres|Provide sample session histogram and P50/P95 lengths|2026-09-19
Evan Park|Share security requirements doc and KMS architecture diagram|2026-09-21
next_steps: Jordan to share Optimize sandbox + cost spreadsheet
Customer to provide session length histogram and sample prompt set
Schedule security follow-up with Redwood security engineer (target week of 9/28)
Plan 2-week pilot on dedicated pool if sims meet targets
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-17
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 38 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Kayla (CTO), Miguel (ML Eng), Evan (SRE), Rosa (Prod)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda — we want to validate the kv prefetch hypothesis we talked about in the email, walk through the Optimize sandbox, run a couple cost sims, and talk deployment constraints. priya will lead the technical bits.

[00:22] Kayla: Yep sounds good. high level we're trying to figure out if session-level caching will actually save us money without degrading latency for our agent product. we have a lot of short sessions but also some longer multi-turns.

[00:35] Priya: great. quick clarifier — when you say session-level caching, do you mean prefix caching (shared prefix across user messages) or full KV cache where we persist key/value states per session? because the tradeoffs are different.

[00:48] Miguel: We mean the KV per session approach — basically warm the KV cache based on the first 1-2 system prompts and some common user scaffolding. our suspicion is that 30–40% of tokens on subsequent turns are stable.

[01:05] Priya: ok that makes sense. i'll show the sandbox and then we'll flip to the cost spreadsheet. quick note — some words in the plan said 'prefetch' and 'sessionization' interchangeably, they're related but prefetch is an optimization to proactively fill kv before the next request.

[01:25] Rosa: also, security — we need to confirm that whatever caching you do doesn't persist PII. can kv entries be scoped and TTL'ed?

[01:34] Jordan: short answer yes — we support ttl and scoping, and in Private deployments you can hook into your KMS for envelope encryption. we'll share the security doc after.

[01:45] Priya: jumping into the console — (screen share) — here's the Optimize sandbox. first panel is the workload picker, you can choose your sequence distribution. i've preloaded a Cerulean profile with p50=48 tokens, p95=640 tokens based on the sample you gave last month, but Miguel feel free to drop your real histogram.

[02:13] Miguel: cool, let me swap that to our latest — (typing noise) — ok new values loaded.

[02:26] Priya: perfect. nav to the Cache tab — we have two levers: prefix cache window size (how many tokens at the start of each session we prefer to keep in fast KV), and prefetch probability / warm-up concurrency (how many sessions we proactively warm per minute). you can also choose eviction TTL or strict session affinity.

[02:52] Evan: question — what's the impact on latency if we warm too many sessions? will it steal GPU cycles?

[03:01] Priya: good question. there are two cost buckets — the prefetch/warms which are extra generation tokens (cost immediate) and the reduced per-turn generation because KV hits avoid re-evaluating prefixes. if your latency SLO is tight, we recommend low concurrency warm-ups and prefer asynchronous prefetching in background paths, or routing to slightly cheaper model variants for warms.

[03:28] Kayla: what's the guidance for routing — we sometimes fall back to smaller models when latency spikes. does the sandbox simulate that?

[03:36] Priya: yes, you can configure fallback policies. the sim will run a scenario where if latency exceeds X ms, requests are routed to a lower-cost model and the cost spreadsheet will show both the savings and potential quality regression risk.

[03:52] Jordan: quick real-talk — many customers are surprised that naive prefetching increases short-term token spend but reduces long-run per-turn cost. the spreadsheet will show cumulative token delta across a 30-day window.

[04:05] Priya: demoing the cost sim now — i've set three workload buckets: bursty short chats (60% of requests, mean 30 tokens), mixed (30%, mean 150 tokens), and long sessions (10%, mean 1200 tokens). baseline is no caching, then try prefix-only caching, and full KV-prefetch at varying concurrency.

[04:33] (sound of mouse clicks)

[04:40] Priya: results — prefix-only saved ~12% total tokens in this mix, KV-prefetch with moderate warms saved ~28% but required ~5% additional upfront warm tokens. p95 latency stayed within the 350ms budget for the mixed scenario but bumped for the long sessions when warms coincided with peak concurrency.

[05:05] Miguel: that's interesting, the 28% matches our back-of-envelope. what about cost per 1M requests?

[05:12] Priya: spreadsheet view — (shared) — for 1M requests with your distribution, baseline monthly token cost is $X (placeholder), prefix-only drops it to ~0.88X, KV-prefetch optimized drops to ~0.72X after amortization. i've left the currency and model unit prices editable.

[05:32] Rosa: can you explain the amortization? is that across cache hits?

[05:38] Priya: yeah — think of amortization as the ratio of warm tokens spent to saved tokens over subsequent turns. if sessions are short and don't return, warms waste tokens. if sessions return many times, warms pay off quickly. the simulator computes amortization factor from your session return rate.

[05:58] Evan: from an infra perspective we care about KV storage size and eviction. how big are entries typically?

[06:05] Priya: entries are roughly proportional to prefix tokens times kv-per-token size; for a 1k token prefix you're looking at X MB of KV per session (demo note: numbers fuzzed in transcript). we support TTL and LRU eviction policies; for on-prem you can control node sizes.

[06:25] Kayla: security follow-up — is KV content encrypted at rest and in transit? who holds keys?

[06:33] Jordan: yes — hosted offers envelope encryption with Redwood-managed keys, Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM. we'll send the SOC2 artifact as well. i flagged this for the security doc.

[06:46] Miguel: what about consistency if we have geo routing — sessions might land on different nodes.

[06:52] Priya: we do session affinity options. for global scale you can either pin sessions to a region or replicate the KV to nearby readers, depends on latency vs cost. the sandbox assumes single-region for simplicity but you can toggle replication in advanced settings.

[07:10] (pause)

[07:18] Priya: i'm going to run a tailored sim now — switching to your dataset profile and increasing prefetch concurrency to 20 warms/min and ttl to 45 minutes. this will show a higher warm cost but better hit rate for multi-turns.

[07:36] (typing)

[07:45] Priya: results posting… ok — hit rate jumps from 18% to 64% on returning sessions; net token savings go positive after ~6 turns on average. p95 latency stays ok for mixed workload but note long sessions saw a bump during a co-located warm window.

[08:05] Miguel: can we throttle warms to low-traffic windows? we have off-peak periods where warms could be scheduled.

[08:11] Priya: absolutely — scheduler supports windowed warms and rate-limiting. many customers warm during predicted activity for specific cohorts.

[08:20] Kayla: ok jumping to objections — if we move to dedicated pools, do we lose the autoscaling cushion for warms?

[08:28] Jordan: dedicated pools have configurable burst capacity; you can reserve headroom for warms or allow dynamic spillover to hosted during spikes. contract parameters vary.

[08:38] Rosa: pricing ask — can we get an example committed plan for ~50M token/mo with dedicated?

[08:43] Jordan: yes we'll include a starter quote in the follow-up.

[08:47] Priya: quick technical deep-dive piece — how we implement KV at runtime: we store key/value for transformer kv caches with optimized kernels, we manage continuous batching for the decode path and avoid re-serializing prefixes when there's a hit. small spelling note — our internal runtime product is sometimes labeled 'Redwood Infer' in older docs, that's the same thing.

[09:11] Evan: do you expose metrics for warm hit rates and amortization? we need that in our observability stack.

[09:17] Priya: yes — Console exposes per-route metrics: warm attempts, successful hits, amortization factor, added latency, and token delta. we also emit traces for warm flows.

[09:29] Miguel: one risk — hallucination drift if we serve older cached context. how do you ensure freshness?

[09:36] Priya: two mechanisms — TTL and version tags. you can attach a prompt checksum or version; on model or prompt updates you can flush matching KV namespaces. the Optimize sim includes a churn scenario to measure stale-hit risk.

[09:55] Kayla: are there any customers with similar scale doing this in production?

[09:59] Jordan: yes — a few mid-market chat platforms and a fintech using session caches. names i can't say on this call but we'll share anonymized case studies.

[10:10] Priya: back to the sandbox — i'm exporting the run into the spreadsheet and annotating the lines where warms flip net-positive. sending in chat now.

[10:18] (link posted)

[10:23] Rosa: saw it. two questions on spreadsheet — what internal multiplier do you use for model token cost and do you include request overhead?

[10:30] Priya: we include model unit price + 8% infra overhead by default, but that's editable. request overhead (JSON payload, network) is captured as a separate line item you can toggle.

[10:38] Miguel: can you rerun with our model variant set? we use a quantized 4-bit variant and we've seen different cost behavior.

[10:44] Priya: sure — i'll run one sim now with a q4 model pricing and a slightly higher per-token latency.

[10:55] (typing)

[11:03] Priya: ok updated. savings are slightly lower in percentage terms because q4 warms are cheaper but decode savings are proportionally smaller. still net-positive for multi-turn heavy cohorts.

[11:18] Kayla: excellent. last piece — timeline. we want to decide by end of September whether to run a pilot. what's realistic?

[11:26] Jordan: timeline: once we get your session histogram and security checklist, we can provision a sandbox pilot in ~1 week, run a 2-week pilot, then review results. so decision by end of month is tight but doable.

[11:39] Kayla: good — we'll send the histogram today.

[11:43] Jordan: recap / next steps — i'll send the sandbox link and annotated spreadsheet (action: Jordan), priya will run two additional sims with your real distribution (action: Priya), Miguel and Evan to share histograms and security prefs (actions: Miguel, Evan). we'll target security follow-up the week of 9/28.

[11:58] Rosa: thanks, appreciate the demo.

[12:02] Jordan: thanks all. meeting end.
